item.title: Crime increases by 11% in August; theft, assault and burglary most prevalent
item.description: Theft, assault causing actual bodily harm and burglary were the three most prevalent offences recorded across Fiji in August, with overall crime increasing by 11 percent compared to the same month last year. The Fiji Police Force says a total of 352 theft cases were recorded, followed by 230 cases of assault causing actual bodily harm and 157 burglary cases.
item.content:encoded:
Theft, assault causing actual bodily harm and burglary were the three most prevalent offences recorded across Fiji in August, with overall crime increasing by 11 percent compared to the same month last year.

The Fiji Police Force says a total of 352 theft cases were recorded, followed by 230 cases of assault causing actual bodily harm and 157 burglary cases.

Police say theft cases were highest in the Western Division with 134 cases, followed by the North with 98, South with 50, East with 48 and Central with 22.

They say most theft cases involved unattended items and cash, while 36 reports involved the theft of livestock and animals.

The majority of offenders were men aged between 18 and 35 years.

For assault causing actual bodily harm, the Western Division recorded the highest number with 82 cases, followed by South with 57, East with 49 and North with 34.

Most of these cases were domestic-related, with men aged between 18 and 35 years making up the majority of alleged offenders.

Burglary cases were highest in the Southern Division, which recorded 66 of the 157 cases, followed by the Western Division with 58, East with 15, North with 14 and Central with four.

The majority of alleged offenders in burglary cases were also males aged between 18 and 35 years.

Meanwhile, there were 89 cases of unlawful possession of illicit drugs recorded in August , with 36 in the Western Division, 19 in the North, 14 in Central, 13 in South and seven in the East.

Most of the drug-related cases involved marijuana, while a smaller number involved methamphetamine.

Criminal intimidation was also among the top five offences, with 75 cases recorded nationwide.

The Western Division recorded 21 cases, followed by the North with 18, South and East with 17 each, and Central with two.

Despite the year-on-year increase, overall crime in August decreased by six percent compared to July 2026.

Police say operations will increase the tempo of proactive community policing initiatives, with a particular focus on young people aged between 18 and 35 years.

There will also be increased enforcement of minor offences which can often lead to other crimes, alongside proactive crime prevention awareness.

item.title: Benzathine will not treat influenza - Dr Lalabalavu, Dr Maharaj
item.description: Following an increase in influenza cases, Health Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu says benzathine injections will not be effective in treating influenza because the illness is caused by a virus, while benzathine is used to treat bacterial infections. Dr Lalabalavu made the comments after well-known doctor Rajesh Maharaj raised concerns about the misuse of benzathine and other antibiotics during
item.content:encoded:
Following an increase in influenza cases, Health Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu says benzathine injections will not be effective in treating influenza because the illness is caused by a virus, while benzathine is used to treat bacterial infections.

Dr Lalabalavu made the comments after well-known doctor Rajesh Maharaj raised concerns about the misuse of benzathine and other antibiotics during Fiji’s current influenza outbreak.

Dr Maharaj says over the years he has seen a pattern during viral outbreaks, including dengue, where patients request antibiotics and some doctors prescribe them for flu-like illnesses.

He says antibiotics such as amoxicillin and benzathine are commonly used in Fiji, but this is not the correct approach.

Dr Maharaj says it is not the patient who should decide whether an antibiotic or injection is needed, but the doctor.

Responding to the concerns, Dr Lalabalavu says benzathine will not have any effect on influenza because it does not treat viral infections.

He says people should focus on proper care, including rest, staying hydrated and allowing the body time to recover.

The Minister is also urging people who are sick to stay home, saying they can easily spread the illness to their co-workers if they continue going to work while unwell.

item.title: More than 4,900 people affected by water shortages in Yasawa as Govt plans assistance
item.description: Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu says assessments in Yasawa have found that four of the five tikina are among the most affected by the prolonged dry weather. These are Nacula, Naviti, Yasawa and Viwa, covering 23 villages, 1,378 households and an estimated 4,965 people.
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu says assessments in Yasawa have found that four of the five tikina are among the most affected by the prolonged dry weather.

These are Nacula, Naviti, Yasawa and Viwa, covering 23 villages, 1,378 households and an estimated 4,965 people.

The water shortage is also affecting essential services, including eight nursing stations, 10 primary schools, two secondary schools and two infant schools.

Bulitavu says the Ministry will now make arrangements to supply water to the affected villages based on the assessment findings.

He says the Ministry is working with the Government Shipping Service to secure a vessel to transport water to the affected maritime communities.

Privately owned barges and other suitable vessels are also being considered for the operation.

Bulitavu says if a suitable vessel is confirmed, the water supply operation could begin as early as next week.

He says the Ministry is also working on assistance for Batiki and Taveuni, where communities have reported water supply problems due to the prolonged dry conditions.
